pr.title: Fix more `ty::Error` ICEs in MIR passes
pr.description:
Fixes #120791 - Add a check for `ty::Error` in the `ByMove` coroutine pass
Fixes #120816 - Add a check for `ty::Error` in the MIR validator

Also a drive-by fix for a FIXME I had asked oli to add

r? oli-obk

processing.reason: The historical difference is confined to the error-recovery path. The original `ByMoveBody` pass assumes the capture-struct local is `ty::Coroutine` and reaches `bug!()` (an ICE/panic) when that type references `ty::Error`; the corrected pass checks `coroutine_ty.references_error()` and returns early. On all non-error inputs both versions perform the same by-move/by-mut body construction and produce identical results. The only distinguishing input is one where the original aborts, so there is no pair of both-defined successful executions that return different numeric/boolean/character values. Modeling the ICE as an alternate `Result`/status value, or converting it into a non-panic return, would manufacture behavior not present in the historical original and would not be a source-grounded semantic counterexample. Therefore no valid `test_program_pair` can be constructed for this fix.

analysis.originalLogic: In `ByMoveBody::run_pass`, the pass reads `body.local_decls[ty::CAPTURE_STRUCT_LOCAL].ty` and assumes it is always `ty::Coroutine(_, args)`, using `let ty::Coroutine(_, args) = *coroutine_ty.kind() else { bug!() };` before building the coroutine by-move body. This assumption ignores that earlier diagnostics can leave the coroutine type tainted with `ty::Error`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Historically, the pass continued into coroutine by-move rewriting for an error-tainted body and reached `bug!()` when the capture-struct local's type was not a valid `ty::Coroutine`, causing an ICE instead of allowing the already-emitted diagnostic to stand. The corrected behavior is to check `coroutine_ty.references_error()` and return from the pass before attempting the `ty::Coroutine` downcast.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies for async closures/coroutines that contain type-checking or writeback errors, specifically an async closure whose capture-struct local type is `ty::Error` or otherwise references an error. The added UI case uses a 2021-edition async closure body containing an unresolved call.
analysis.summary: `ByMoveBody` must skip coroutine by-move rewriting when the coroutine capture-struct local type references `ty::Error`; otherwise an unresolved name in an async closure body can turn a normal E0425 diagnostic into an ICE.
analysis.trigger: An async closure body is tainted by an earlier error, such as `used_fn()` being unresolvable, and `ByMoveBody` runs on the resulting `mir_const` body whose `ty::CAPTURE_STRUCT_LOCAL` type is not a valid `ty::Coroutine`.
preconditions: The crate enables `#![feature(async_closure)]`; the regression test uses `// edition:2021`.
The async closure body contains an error such as an unresolved function call, so the coroutine type references `ty::Error`.
The `ByMoveBody` MIR pass is reached for that coroutine/closure body, as during `mir_const` preparation.
pitfalls: Do not assume `body.local_decls[ty::CAPTURE_STRUCT_LOCAL].ty` is always `ty::Coroutine`; error recovery can make it `ty::Error`.
Checking only after forcing the `ty::Coroutine` downcast is too late: use `references_error()` before the `let ... else`.
The early return must not suppress the original diagnostic; the regression test still expects the normal `E0425` error and no ICE.
Changing the panic message to include `{body:#?}` is diagnostic-only and is not the semantic fix.
This is error-path robustness, not a valid-program optimization; the distinguishing input is introducing or removing the unresolved call in an async closure body.
analysis.testStrategy: Add or extend a UI test under `tests/ui/async-await/async-closures/` with `// edition:2021`, `#![feature(async_closure)]`, and an async closure body calling an unresolved function. Run rustc with ordinary diagnostics and assert only the expected `error[E0425]: cannot find function ...` plus the single-error abort, with no `internal compiler error`; also compare with an otherwise identical async closure without the unresolved call. The supplied regression test is `tests/ui/async-await/async-closures/tainted-body.rs` with a matching `.stderr`. No compiler was built here, so this is test design guidance rather than an execution claim.
